architecture.browser: The trained classifier, extraction rules, and follow-up transitions run in the browser.
architecture.firebase: Firebase Hosting serves the app. Firebase Authentication signs users in. Cloud Firestore stores account care spaces.
architecture.rules: Firestore rules validate ownership, immutable source fields, versions, and quotas. They do not independently validate the full clinical follow-up transition workflow.
architecture.save: Saving the current demo to an account preserves its edits.
architecture.limitations: A user-entered clinician name or completion is a report, not verified clinical attestation. The MVP has no EHR integration or proven health benefit.

left.title: Why this matters
left.body: Leaving hospital can leave unfinished work: a pending result, a repeat test, or a referral. In a 2005 study of 2,644 discharges at two academic hospitals, 41% of patients had results return after discharge.<super>1</super>

left.title: What the MVP does
left.body:
Review the source. Paste text or import a text PDF. Model and rules suggest tasks. Inspect every sentence, including omissions.

Name the tracker. Confirm each follow-up, the person tracking it, and any date. Unclear source details remain visible.

Record the ending. Result receipt stays separate from user-reported clinician review. The history retains the reported outcome.

left.title: A plan people can use
left.body: Save the edited demo to an account. Briefs include unconverted source text. Calendar/JSON exports keep the record portable. Anita and Maya are fictional.

right.title: Historical evaluation
right.body:
On 20 known synthetic documents, 33 of 34 proposals matched annotations (97.1% precision), and 33 of 44 expected actions were found (75% recall).

Known fixtures reused during fixes, not held-out or clinical validation. No measured model improvement over rules alone.

right.title: A business to test
right.body:
First buyer hypothesis: a primary-care or transitions coordinator already chasing discharge follow-up.

$149/month for 100 care episodes is a pricing hypothesis. Measure preparation time, corrections, and willingness to pay.

right.title: Built for a narrow workflow
right.body: Model and workflow run in the browser. Firebase provides hosting, sign-in, and saved plans. 57 live Firebase checks passed. Owner isolation and persistence were verified. No paid inference API or proven health benefit.

one_page.footer: Prototype tested with synthetic data. Patient deployment requires clinical and security review.

slides.notes: Roy CL et al. Patient safety concerns arising from test results that return after hospital discharge. Ann Intern Med. 2005. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16027454/ . The discharges were in 2004 at two academic hospitals. This is historical workflow context, not today's global prevalence. The 2025 SAFER Test Results Reporting and Follow-Up guide provides additional workflow context: https://healthit.gov/resources/2025-safer-guide-test-results-reporting-and-follow-up/ . Neither source endorses Looplight or establishes its benefit.

slides.notes: The desktop and mobile captures show the real Firebase application using fictional Anita/Maya data. Original screenshot bytes are retained with editable native crops. The app accepts pasted text and text-based PDFs, exposes all source sentences, and requires task confirmation before tracking. The current demo can be saved to an account with its edits preserved. slides.notes: Follow-up transition logic runs in the browser. Firestore rules validate ownership, immutable source fields, versions, and quotas; they do not independently validate the full follow-up transition workflow. The user records clinician review and outcome. A clinician name is not verified identity or signed attestation. A tracker is the person following up, not an assignment of clinical responsibility. The actual Firebase result-detail capture shows source evidence and unresolved details, not clinician-verified evidence.

slides.title: Measured on known synthetic fixtures
slides.context: Historical evaluation on 20 known synthetic documents.
slides.caveat: Reused during fixes. Not held-out or clinical validation.
slides.next: The next evaluation needs independently annotated documents.
slides.notes: Historical development report, not a new Firebase deployment benchmark: 20 synthetic document fixtures, 44 expected actions, 34 proposals, 33 matches. Precision 33/34 = 97.1%; recall 33/44 = 75%. The initial development result was 84.2% precision and 72.7% recall; fixes were evaluated on the same known fixtures. This is not an untouched holdout, clinician-annotated real-world evaluation, or evidence of health benefit. No model uplift over rules alone has been demonstrated. Separate classifier evidence, if judges ask: 225 original synthetic training examples, 50 separately authored synthetic challenge examples, 82% raw five-category accuracy, macro F1 about 0.816, 44/50 abstentions. Do not conflate sentence classification with document-level extraction or clinical safety. Firebase deployment checks are separate from this historical extraction evaluation.

slides.caveat: Illustrative inputs, before review and implementation costs. No observed ROI.
slides.notes: The price and savings inputs are hypotheses, not customer research. $149 per coordinator account/month for 100 episodes is a proposed experiment. No revenue, willingness-to-pay evidence, customer validation, or observed time saving is claimed. Five minutes x 100 / 60 x $35 = $291.67 before review and implementation costs. Inference runs in the browser without a paid model API; hosting, storage, support, security review, clinical governance, and bandwidth remain costs. Shared team workflows are future work. Related products include SeamlessMD, Memora/Commure, Eon, and care-management platforms. Source grounding alone is not a demonstrated moat.

slides.caveat: Prototype tested with synthetic data. No clinical validation or proven health benefit.
slides.notes: Firebase Hosting, Firebase Authentication, and Cloud Firestore replace the previous hosting/account stack. Model inference, task extraction, and workflow transitions execute in the browser. Firestore security rules enforce ownership, immutable source fields, versions, and quotas. They do not provide independent server-side clinical transition validation. The current demo-save flow preserves edits in the account. The build owner supplied 57 passed live Firebase checks and verified owner isolation and persistence. Google sign-in and edited-demo account-save persistence were verified in the GUI. Additional UI review continues. No flawless-operation claim is made. Proposed next work is a governed retrospective review with clinician annotation, followed by a supervised pilot. A small pilot cannot prove a causal reduction in readmissions.
